w: Double ramparts and fifty-two towers crown this hilltop citadel above the river Aude, restored stone by stone at the end of the 19th century by architect Eugene Viollet-le-Duc after centuries of decay. UNESCO listed it in 1997 as one of Europe's most complete surviving medieval fortress towns.
s: Double ramparts, fifty-two towers, one restored skyline.
_facts: Medieval citadel on a hill on the right bank of the Aude, in Carcassonne, Aude department, Occitania
Restored at the end of the 19th century by theorist and architect Eugene Viollet-le-Duc
Added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1997 for its testimony to medieval fortress-town architecture and planning

w: Built in the 13th century as a humble parish church, Saint-Michel took a beating in 14th-century warfare and was rebuilt fortified, its buttresses doubling as defence. An 1803 decree made it cathedral, bumping the older Saint-Nazaire down to basilica - it still serves worshippers today.
s: Rebuilt as a fortress, then made a cathedral by decree.
_facts: Built in the 13th century as a parish church dedicated to Saint Michael
Rebuilt as a fortified church after war damage in the 14th century
Elevated to cathedral status in 1803, replacing the earlier cathedral now known as the Basilica of St. Nazaire and St. Celse; used today by the Priestly Fraternity of Saint Peter

n: Basilica of St. Nazaire and St. Celse
w: Half Romanesque, half Gothic, this minor basilica sits inside the citadel walls and served as Carcassonne's cathedral until 1803, when the honour passed across town to Saint-Michel. Demoted but not diminished: still a national monument, its stone rounding one era into the next mid-nave.
s: Carcassonne's first cathedral, demoted but not diminished.
_facts: Roman Catholic minor basilica located inside the citadel of Carcassonne, a French national monument
Built in the Gothic-Romanesque architectural tradition
Served as Carcassonne's cathedral until 1803, when the seat moved to Saint-Michel and this church was redesignated a basilica

w: After wildfires scorched these hills in 1985, engineers dammed the valley and let it flood - creating Carcassonne Plage, a sheet of water where none existed before. Ducks patrol reed-fringed shallows, rental boats potter about, and a crazy-golf course sits by the shore. The lake still draws bathers each summer.
s: A lake built from a 1985 wildfire scar.
_facts: Artificial lake near Carcassonne, created by a 23-metre dam built in 1988 after severe forest fires in 1985
Also known as Carcassonne Plage; surface area 180,000 sq m, fed by the Montirat, Bazalac and Mitge creeks
Popular recreation area with supervised bathing, boat rental, picnic areas and a crazy golf course; bathing was suspended in 2005 due to algal blooms
